notes: Friendly and fine almost everywhere, also with staff. More formal: Guten Tag.
The polite daytime hello. Bavaria and Austria say Grüß Gott, Switzerland Grüezi, the north Moin.

examples.tl: Guten Tag, ich habe eine Reservierung.
examples.en: Good day, I have a reservation.

notes: Until about 10 or 11 a.m. Often shortened to just 'Morgen!'

examples.tl: Guten Morgen! Gibt es schon Frühstück?
examples.en: Good morning! Is breakfast being served yet?

notes: From about 6 p.m., for example when you walk into a restaurant.

examples.tl: Guten Abend, haben Sie noch einen Tisch frei?
examples.en: Good evening, do you still have a table free?

notes: Only when someone is going to bed, never as a greeting.
The everyday goodbye, fine with shop staff too. In Bavaria and Austria you also hear Servus.
The formal goodbye. On the phone: Auf Wiederhören. Bavaria and Austria: Auf Wiederschauen.

examples.en: Thank you very much and goodbye!

notes: Also the reply to danke (you're welcome) and what staff say when handing you something.
Trap: answering an offer with just 'danke' usually means 'no, thanks'. Say 'ja, bitte' to accept.

examples.en: Thank you very much for the information!

notes: Reply to thanks, and said when handing something over. As a question from staff (Bitte schön?) it means 'What can I get you?'

examples.en: Thank you very much! – You're welcome.

notes: To get attention, to squeeze past, or for a small apology. Often swallowed to 'Tschuldigung'.

examples.en: Excuse me, may I get past?

notes: A real apology or sympathy. For bumping into someone, Entschuldigung is enough.

examples.tl: Tut mir leid, ich bin zu spät.

notes: 'Doch' is the yes that contradicts a negative question: Sprechen Sie kein Deutsch? – Doch!

examples.tl: Entschuldigung, ich verstehe nicht. Können Sie langsamer sprechen?
examples.en: Sorry, I don't understand. Can you speak more slowly?

notes: Ask before switching to English: it is more polite, and most younger Germans will say yes.

examples.tl: Entschuldigung, sprechen Sie Englisch? – Ja, ein bisschen.
examples.en: Excuse me, do you speak English? – Yes, a little.

tl: Ich spreche nur ein bisschen Deutsch
en: I only speak a little German
accept: I speak only a little German
I just speak a little German

examples.tl: Ich spreche nur ein bisschen Deutsch. Können wir Englisch sprechen?
examples.en: I only speak a little German. Can we speak English?

examples.tl: Können Sie das bitte wiederholen? Ich habe es nicht verstanden.
examples.en: Could you repeat that, please? I didn't understand it.

examples.tl: Langsamer, bitte. Mein Deutsch ist nicht so gut.
examples.en: Slower, please. My German is not that good.

notes: The polite way to say you did not catch something. A bare 'Was?' sounds rude.

examples.tl: Wie bitte? Ich habe Sie nicht verstanden.

tl: Wie sagt man das auf Deutsch?
en: How do you say that in German?
accept: How do you say this in German?

examples.en: How do you say 'receipt' in German?

notes: Germans say this constantly to agree or confirm: 'Genau!'

examples.en: Very good, thank you very much!

notes: 'Nicht schlecht!' (not bad) is real praise in German.

examples.tl: Ein Bier und ein Wasser, bitte.
examples.en: A beer and a water, please.

notes: Tacked onto the end of a sentence (..., oder?) it means 'right?'

examples.tl: Das Zimmer ist klein, aber sauber.
examples.en: The room is small but clean.

notes: Takes the dative: mit dem Zug, mit der Karte. Often without an article: mit Karte, mit Milch.
Takes the accusative. Handy for orders: ohne Zwiebeln (onions), ohne Fleisch, ohne Eis.
Negates verbs and adjectives. Nouns are negated with kein: kein Fleisch.
Negates nouns, with the endings of ein: kein Zucker, keine Milch, keinen Platz (masculine object).
There = dort, or in speech usually da: da drüben = over there.
Not capitalized except at the start of a sentence.
Always capitalized. For staff and strangers; the verb ends in -en: Sie haben, Sie können. du is for friends, children and peers who offer it.
Only for questions about time. The other question words: wo (where), wer (who), warum (why), wie (how).

examples.tl: Die Leute hier sind sehr freundlich.
examples.en: The people here are very friendly.

notes: Means 'understood' or 'okay'. As a question (Alles klar?) it is a casual 'everything okay?'

examples.tl: Der Zug fährt von Gleis 5. – Alles klar, danke!
examples.en: The train leaves from platform 5. – All right, thanks!

examples.tl: Einen Moment, bitte, ich suche meine Fahrkarte.
examples.en: One moment, please, I'm looking for my ticket.

examples.tl: Ich weiß nicht, wo das Hotel ist.
examples.en: I don't know where the hotel is.

notes: Point and say 'das' when you do not know the word. Also the neuter article: das Bier.
'Gerne!' from staff = with pleasure / you're welcome. Verb + gern = like doing: Ich wandere gern.

examples.tl: Möchten Sie noch etwas? – Ja, gern.
examples.en: Would you like anything else? – Yes, please.
